## Core Overview
- Primary purpose: Organize, summarize, and display raw data using tables, charts, histograms, and graphs to make large data sets manageable and interpretable.
- Fundamental themes: Objectives of data presentation, types of frequency distributions, cumulative frequencies, relative frequencies, and graphical representations like histograms and frequency polygons.

## Key Concepts & Formulas
- Objectives of Data Presentation:
  - Simplify raw data: Makes large amounts of raw data easier to understand and analyze.
  - Remove complexity: Removes unnecessary details and highlights important features.
  - Make comparison easier: Helps compare different data sets and draw conclusions.
  - Help in statistical analysis: Divides data into similar groups to identify similarities and differences.
- Types of Frequency Distribution:
  - Ungrouped Frequency Distribution: Uses individual data values and their corresponding frequencies.
  - Grouped Frequency Distribution: Divides data into classes or intervals with associated frequencies.
- Essential Formulas (Plain Text):
  - Percentage Frequency = (Frequency / Total Frequency) * 100
  - Relative Frequency (r.f) = Observed Frequency / Total Frequency
  - Cumulative Relative Frequency (c.r.f) = Cumulative Frequency / Total Frequency
  - Range = Maximum Value - Minimum Value
  - Number of Classes (c) = 1 + 3.3 * log(n)
  - Class Width (h) = Range / Number of Classes
- Cumulative Frequency Distribution:
  - Shows the running total of frequencies up to each class by adding the frequencies of all preceding classes including the current class.
- Graphical Methods:
  - Histogram: Uses adjacent bars representing class boundaries on the x-axis and frequencies on the y-axis.
  - Frequency Polygon / Curve: Connects the midpoints of the tops of the histogram bars to show the continuous distribution of data.

## Exam Takeaways
- Always verify that the last cumulative frequency equals the total sample size (n).
- Class boundaries must be continuous (e.g., 85.5 - 90.5) when constructing histograms and frequency distributions to avoid gaps.
- Memorize the formula for determining the number of classes: c = 1 + 3.3 * log(n), where n is the total number of observations.
- Be prepared to convert raw data into a complete frequency table including class limits, class boundaries, midpoints (xi), tallies, frequencies, relative frequencies, cumulative frequencies, and cumulative relative frequencies.
